Abstract

We predict the redshift of galaxies, a measure of their distance, from their brightness in the five SDSS filters. The data are 120 galaxies from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (DR18) with spectroscopic redshifts between 0.025 and 0.221. They were cleaned with AI assistance and split into 100 training and 20 test galaxies. Four supervised models (linear regression, k-nearest neighbours, random forest and support vector regression) were tuned by repeated cross-validation in R and compared with a mean-prediction baseline. In cross-validation the best model was M4 SVR (RMSE 0.0217 vs 0.0440 for the baseline). On the held-out test set the best model was M3 Random Forest (RMSE 0.0318, σNMAD 0.0276, no catastrophic outliers). The colour g − r is by far the most important predictor, and predicted redshift rises steadily with it. This is the signature of the 4000 Å break moving through the g filter as galaxies recede. This is version v2 of the analysis: the original 100 galaxies (v1) plus 20 new galaxies from a second SDSS pull, all added to the training set. Scored on the same 20 test galaxies as v1, the extra data gave a clear improvement for M2 k-NN and no clear change for the others (paired bootstrap).

1 Introduction and physics background

1.1 Redshift

Light from a receding galaxy is stretched to longer wavelengths:

\[ z = \frac{\lambda_{\text{obs}} - \lambda_{\text{emit}}}{\lambda_{\text{emit}}}, \qquad \lambda_{\text{obs}} = (1+z)\,\lambda_{\text{emit}}. \]

At low redshift, Hubble’s law gives \(v \approx cz = H_0 d\), so the redshift measures distance.

1.2 Spectroscopic versus photometric redshift

A spectroscopic redshift comes from the shift of spectral lines. It is very precise but slow and expensive to obtain. A photometric redshift estimates z from the brightness in a few broad filters. It is less precise but works for billions of galaxies, which is essential for surveys such as LSST, Euclid and DES. Galaxies that have both measurements let us learn the mapping from photometry to redshift: a supervised regression problem.

1.3 Why colours encode redshift: the 4000 Å break

Older stellar populations produce a sharp drop in galaxy spectra blueward of 4000 Å. As z increases, the break appears at \(4000(1+z)\) Å and removes flux from the bluer filter, so the colour (magnitude difference) between filters changes. Figure F20 shows that, for the redshift range of this sample, the break always lies inside the g band. We therefore expect g − r to redden with redshift and to be the most informative feature. The r magnitude adds distance information because, in a flux-limited sample, more distant galaxies look fainter (inverse-square law).

Figure F20. Observed wavelength of the 4000 Å break, 4000(1 + z) Å (black line), over the SDSS filter bands (shaded: effective wavelength ± FWHM/2, approximate). The grey band marks this sample (z = 0.025–0.221), where the break lies at 4098–4885 Å, inside the g band. It would leave g only at z ≈ 0.34.

1.4 Aim and hypotheses

Can a galaxy’s colours predict its redshift? We test four hypotheses:

  • H1: g − r is the most important predictor.
  • H2: predicted redshift rises monotonically with g − r.
  • H3: non-linear models (k-NN, random forest, SVR) beat linear regression.
  • H4: all models beat the mean-prediction baseline.

2 Data

2.1 Acquisition

120 random galaxies were retrieved from SDSS DR18 with a SkyServer SQL query (data/sql/sdss_query.sql) by R/01_acquire.R. The query keeps spectroscopically confirmed galaxies with reliable redshifts (zWarning = 0), clean photometry, the Main Galaxy Sample flux limit 14 ≤ r ≤ 17.77, 0.01 < z < 0.5 and magnitude errors below 0.2. Magnitudes are corrected for Milky Way dust (dered_*). The raw file is frozen and recorded with an MD5 checksum in data/raw/ACQUISITION.md. For version v2 a second, independent pull of 30 galaxies was made with the identical query (batch 2, data/sql/sdss_query_batch2.sql) and frozen in the same way (data/raw/ACQUISITION_batch2.md).

2.2 AI-assisted inspection and cleaning

Following workflow step 2, an AI assistant (Claude Code) inspected the raw data’s structure, missing and sentinel values, duplicates, ranges and colour outliers, then proposed cleaning rules. The student reviewed every rule. Each rule logs its row counts (Table T02), and every AI interaction is recorded in the appendix. The data contained no missing values, sentinels or duplicates. The colour-outlier rule (median ± 5·MAD) removed 2 galaxies that were blue in all colours. The AI suggested keeping them as probably real star-forming galaxies; the student chose to apply the planned rule. A random sample of 100 galaxies (seed 42) forms the v1 analysis set. For v2, batch 2 went through exactly the same rules (R/utils_clean.R). The colour-outlier rule used the frozen batch-1 median and MAD, so the threshold did not move and no v1 galaxy could be dropped; it removed 2 batch-2 galaxies. Galaxies already present in batch 1 would also have been removed (there were none). 20 of the survivors were drawn at random (seed 42) and appended to the 100 v1 galaxies, giving 120. Table T02 below is the batch-2 log; two-sample KS tests found no difference between batch 2 and batch 1 in redshift, r, g − r or u − g (smallest p = 0.16).

3 Methods

3.1 Features and target

The target is the spectroscopic redshift. The features are the four colours u − g, g − r, r − i, i − z and the r-band magnitude. Colours remove the overall brightness and keep the shape of the spectrum, while r carries the brightness–distance information.

3.2 Train/test split

v2 keeps exactly the 20 test galaxies of v1, so the two versions are compared on the same galaxies (a paired design). All other galaxies (the 80 v1 training galaxies and the 20 new ones) form the 100-galaxy training set. v1 itself used a stratified split on redshift (caret::createDataPartition, seed 42). A two-sample KS test finds no difference between their redshift distributions (D = 0.110, p = 0.980, Figure F07). The test set was not used for any training, tuning or preprocessing decision.

Figure F07. Spectroscopic redshift of the 100 training and 20 test galaxies (histograms, kernel densities and rugs) after a split that keeps v1’s 20 test galaxies and trains on all others. Two-sample KS test: D = 0.110, p = 0.980, so there is no evidence that the two distributions differ.

3.3 Models and tuning

All models use redshift ~ u_g + g_r + r_i + i_z + r and the same 25 resamples (5-fold cross-validation repeated 5 times) on the training set. Hyperparameters were chosen by the lowest mean CV RMSE (Table T03). Centring and scaling were fitted inside each training fold.

Table T03. Hyperparameter grids and selected values.
Model Parameter Search grid Selected
M0 Baseline (none) predicts the training mean —
M1 Linear (none) ordinary least squares —
M2 k-NN k 1, 2, …, 20 11
M3 Random Forest mtry 1, 2, …, 5 5
M3 Random Forest ntree fixed 500
M4 SVR C 2^-2, 2^-1, …, 2^6 32
M4 SVR sigma 0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.5, 1 0.01

3.4 Metrics

With \(\Delta z = (z_{\text{phot}} - z_{\text{spec}})/(1 + z_{\text{spec}})\) we report RMSE, MAE, \(R^2 = 1 - SS_{\text{res}}/SS_{\text{tot}}\), bias = mean(Δz), the robust scatter \(\sigma_{\text{NMAD}} = 1.4826 \times \text{median}(|\Delta z - \text{median}(\Delta z)|)\) and the catastrophic-outlier fraction η = fraction with |Δz| > 0.15. Test metrics carry 95% percentile bootstrap confidence intervals (2000 resamples).

5 Discussion: physics interpretation

5.1 Which features matter and why

Table T06. Feature importance: random-forest permutation importance and standardised linear-regression coefficients with 95% CIs.
Feature RF %IncMSE RF rank LM std. coef. LM CI low LM CI high LM rank
g − r 51.9659 1 0.0606 0.0502 0.0711 1
u − g 13.9259 2 -0.0344 -0.0431 -0.0257 2
r − i 9.8794 3 -0.0009 -0.0093 0.0075 5
r (mag) 7.7328 4 0.0080 0.0028 0.0132 4
i − z 5.4678 5 -0.0104 -0.0181 -0.0028 3

Figure F18. Feature importance. Left: random-forest permutation importance (%IncMSE). Right: standardised linear-regression coefficients with 95% CIs (change in predicted z per 1 SD of each feature). Most important: g − r (RF) and g − r (LM).

Figure F19. Partial dependence of the random-forest redshift prediction on g − r and r − i (training data; rugs show the observed values). Over the observed range, predicted z changes by 0.106 with g − r (Spearman ρ = 0.98).

The random forest ranks g − r first (%IncMSE 51.97), and the partial dependence (Figure F19) shows predicted redshift climbing steadily with g − r. This is the behaviour expected from the 4000 Å break moving redward through the g filter: the galaxy loses flux in g relative to r and its g − r colour reddens. r − i correlates with z on its own (Figure F04) but adds little once g − r is known, because the two colours are strongly correlated (Figure F05).

  • Random-forest ranking: 1. g − r (%IncMSE 52.0); 2. u − g (%IncMSE 13.9); 3. r − i (%IncMSE 9.9); 4. r (mag) (%IncMSE 7.7); 5. i − z (%IncMSE 5.5).
  • Most important feature: g − r (random forest), g − r (largest |standardised coefficient| in the linear model).
  • r magnitude: RF rank 4 of 5; LM coefficient 0.0080 [95% CI 0.0028, 0.0132]: positive, so fainter galaxies are predicted at higher z, as the inverse-square law expects.
  • u − g: almost no correlation with z on its own (training r = 0.06) but RF rank 2 and LM coefficient -0.0344 [-0.0431, -0.0257] at fixed g − r. Interpretation: u − g traces galaxy type (old/red vs star-forming/blue), which lets the models tell an intrinsically red galaxy from one reddened by redshift in g − r.
  • The colours are strongly correlated with each other (F05), so individual linear coefficients can trade off against each other; their CIs are wide.

5.2 Hypotheses

  • H1 (g − r is the most important predictor): supported by both RF and LM.
  • H2 (predicted z rises monotonically with g − r): supported. Spearman ρ of the RF partial-dependence curve = 0.98 (threshold 0.8).
  • H3 (non-linear models beat linear regression): CV partly supported (only M4 SVR beat LM); test partly supported (only M2 k-NN, M3 Random Forest beat LM). CV RMSE: LM 0.0238, k-NN 0.0324, RF 0.0302, SVR 0.0217. Test RMSE: LM 0.0418, k-NN 0.0376, RF 0.0318, SVR 0.0444.
  • H4 (all models beat the mean baseline): CV supported, test supported (point estimates; baseline CV 0.0440, test 0.0457). The test CIs in T05 overlap the baseline for 3 of 4 learners.

5.3 Where the models fail

Cross-validation ranks M4 SVR first, but on the test set M3 Random Forest is best. The difference comes from a few test galaxies whose colours lie outside the range seen in training (2 of 20). For such galaxies the linear model and the near-linear SVR extrapolate and can predict a negative, unphysical redshift (2 predictions below zero in total). A random forest predicts averages of training redshifts and cannot leave the training range, so it is more robust to such galaxies. Every model also pulls the lowest- and highest-redshift galaxies towards the mean redshift (Figure F15), a typical effect of a small training set.

With only 20 test galaxies the confidence intervals in Table T05 overlap strongly, so no model is clearly better than another on this test set. The robust scatter σNMAD of 0.0276 (95% CI 0.0102–0.0421) falls within the ≈ 0.02–0.03 reported for SDSS photo-z trained on hundreds of thousands of galaxies. With only 100 training galaxies and a narrow redshift range this is encouraging, but the wide interval means the comparison is not precise. The learning curves (Figure F12) show the gap between training and test error for each model as the training set grows.

  • Test galaxies with at least one feature outside the training range: 2 of 20.
  • Negative (unphysical) test predictions: 2 (M1 Linear, M4 SVR). Linear and kernel models can extrapolate beyond the training redshifts; random-forest predictions are averages of training redshifts and cannot.
  • Over this sample’s redshift range (0.025–0.221) the 4000 Å break stays inside the g band (F20), so the redshift signal is the break moving within g, which reddens g − r.

6 Effect of 20 more training galaxies: v1 versus v2

Both versions are scored on the same 20 test galaxies, so their difference is estimated with a paired bootstrap: each of 2000 resamples of the test galaxies is scored with both versions, which cancels the galaxy-to-galaxy scatter that makes each version’s own confidence interval in Table T05 so wide.

Model Parameter v1 v2
M0 Baseline (none) — —
M1 Linear (none) — —
M2 k-NN k 8 11
M3 Random Forest mtry 5 5
M3 Random Forest ntree 500 500
M4 SVR C 32 32
M4 SVR sigma 0.01 0.01

  • v1: 100 galaxies (80 train / 20 test). v2: 120 galaxies (100 train / 20 test).

  • The 20 new galaxies come from a second, independent SkyServer pull with the same query (batch 2) and passed the same cleaning rules. They were added to the training set only; the 20 test galaxies are identical in both versions.

  • New galaxies: z = 0.032–0.199 (median 0.094; v1 training median 0.101). KS test against the v1 training set: redshift p = 0.68, g − r p = 0.10, so there is no evidence that they come from a different population.

  • 2 of the 20 new galaxies lie outside the v1 training range in at least one feature, so v2 covers a wider region of colour space. Test galaxies outside the training range: 4 in v1, 2 in v2.

  • With 20 test galaxies, each version’s own RMSE CI is wide (T05). The paired CI removes the shared galaxy-to-galaxy scatter, so it is the right test of whether the extra training data helped.

  • M1 Linear: no clear change (paired 95% CI [-0.0021, +0.0029] includes zero; P(better) = 0.28).

  • M2 k-NN: clear improvement (paired 95% CI [-0.0081, -0.0015] lies below zero).

  • M3 Random Forest: no clear change (paired 95% CI [-0.0049, +0.0027] includes zero; P(better) = 0.76).

  • M4 SVR: no clear change (paired 95% CI [-0.0018, +0.0107] includes zero; P(better) = 0.09).

  • Bias–variance reading: k-NN and the random forest predict from local averages of training galaxies, so with n = 80 their error is dominated by variance (how sparsely the colour–redshift relation is sampled). 25% more galaxies samples it more densely, and the CV-tuned k rose from 8 to 11: with denser data the model can average more neighbours without blurring the relation. Linear regression has 6 parameters and is limited by bias (a straight line through a curved relation), so extra data cannot help it. The tuned SVR kernel is very wide (σ = 0.01), which makes it close to linear, so it behaves like the linear model; its test change is within the noise.

  • Learning curves (F22, v2): from 80 to 100 training galaxies the mean test RMSE changes by M1 Linear -0.0002, M2 k-NN +0.0002, M3 Random Forest -0.0002, M4 SVR +0.0034. No curve is still falling by more than 0.001 in RMSE, so further galaxies of the same kind would give only small gains: the remaining error is set mainly by how much redshift information five broad-band magnitudes carry (intrinsic scatter of the colour–redshift relation), not by the sample size.

7 Limitations

  • Small sample. n = 120 (v2 deliberately goes 20 beyond the brief’s limit of 100, decision D-018; v1 is the brief-compliant version). Real photo-z work uses 105–106 training galaxies.
  • Small test set. With 20 galaxies, metrics have wide confidence intervals and η can only change in steps of 5%.
  • Narrow redshift range. The models are valid only for 0.025 ≤ z ≤ 0.221 and r ≤ 17.77. In this range the break never leaves the g band.
  • Very blue galaxies excluded. The 5·MAD cleaning rule removed galaxies that are blue in every colour, so the models have not learned such objects.
  • Unphysical extrapolation. The linear model and SVR can predict z < 0 for galaxies with colours outside the training range.
  • Unused information. Magnitude errors were not used as weights or inputs.

8 Conclusion

Five-band SDSS photometry predicts galaxy redshift better than a mean-value baseline, even with only 100 training galaxies. On the test set the best model, M3 Random Forest, reaches RMSE 0.0318 against 0.0457 for the baseline. Every learner beats the baseline on the point estimate, but only M3 Random Forest has a 95% confidence interval entirely below it, so with 20 test galaxies the improvement is clear only for that model. The models learn the physics: g − r, which tracks the 4000 Å break moving through the g filter, dominates the predictions, and predicted redshift rises monotonically with it. Smooth models (linear regression, SVR) do best in cross-validation, while the random forest is the most robust on unusual test galaxies because it cannot extrapolate to unphysical values. Adding 20 galaxies (25% more training data) changed the test RMSE by M1 Linear +1.8%, M2 k-NN -12.2%, M3 Random Forest -4.0%, M4 SVR +13.4%. Only M2 k-NN improved beyond the paired uncertainty, and no model got clearly worse. The gain shows up in the local, variance-limited learner, as expected, while the bias-limited linear model is unchanged.

9.0.0.2.2 AI-002 — Data acquisition scripts
  • Date: 2026-10-18
  • Stage: Acquisition (code)

  • Prompt (short): “Write the data collection scripts.”
  • AI output / suggestion:
    • Tested the SkyServer SqlSearch web service with throw-away TOP 3 and TOP 5 queries, outside the repository. Findings: DR18 accepts the project query unchanged and returns all 15 expected columns in about 15 s. The response starts with a #Table1 line before the CSV header. objid values have 19 digits, so they must be read as text. SQL errors come back as HTTP 500 with a JSON ErrorMessage.
    • Wrote R/00_setup.R (packages, SEED, paths, data contract), R/utils_metrics.R, R/utils_plot.R and R/01_acquire.R. The acquisition script downloads via the web service (DR18, then DR17), strips #Table1, checks the header and row count, writes ACQUISITION.md with an MD5 checksum, and on later runs refuses to download again and stops if the raw file’s MD5 has changed (D-015).
    • Added a .here file. The git repository root is the parent folder (Kavya-jini/), so without it here::here() would resolve paths there instead of inside sdss-photoz-r/.
  • Owner decision: Accepted. The owner reviewed the scripts and committed them.
  • Resulting code: files above
  • Effect on data: R/01_acquire.R downloaded 120 rows × 15 columns from DR18 on 2026-10-18 (see data/raw/ACQUISITION.md for the MD5). A second run skipped the download and confirmed the MD5.

9.0.0.2.3 AI-003 — Inspection of the raw data
  • Date: 2026-10-18
  • Stage: Inspection
  • Tool / model: Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5)
  • Input given to AI: output of str(), summary(), NA, sentinel and duplicate counts, colour summaries and MAD outlier counts for data/raw/sdss_raw.csv. The full output is saved in outputs/logs/02_inspection.txt.
  • Prompt (short): “Inspect the raw data and flag anything the cleaning rules must handle.”
  • AI output / suggestion:
    • 120 rows × 15 columns. No NA, no sentinel values (±9999), no duplicate objid, no fully duplicated rows, and no repeated sky positions.
    • All objid values have 19 digits and are intact as text.
    • All magnitudes lie well inside [10, 30] and redshift inside (0, 1). All magnitude errors are below the query’s 0.2 cut.
    • The redshift range (about 0.025–0.22) is narrower than D-005 expected. At these redshifts the 4000 Å break stays inside the g band, which matters for the physics discussion.
    • With the 5·MAD rule, 2 galaxies are flagged, both on i_z: 1237665548892962975 (z = 0.031) and 1237657769630695800 (z = 0.050). Both are blue in all four colours, not just one. The first has typical photometric errors; the second has errors about 2–4× the sample median but well under the 0.2 cut. The AI judged them to be real blue star-forming galaxies rather than bad photometry, since bad photometry usually shifts a single colour.
  • Owner decision: Noted. See AI-004 for how the outliers were handled.
  • Resulting code: inspection block (step 2) of R/02_inspect_clean.R
  • Effect on data: none (inspection only)

9.0.0.2.8 AI-008 — Model training and tuning
  • Date: 2026-10-18
  • Stage: Modelling (code)
  • Tool / model: Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5)
  • Input given to AI: train.csv (via the script). test.csv is used only to score the learning-curve refits after tuning.
  • Prompt (short): “Write and run R/05_train.R (baseline, LM, kNN, RF, SVR with shared repeated-CV folds, T03, T04, F08–F13).”
  • AI output / suggestion:
    • One fixed set of 25 resamples (createMultiFolds, 5-fold × 5, seed 42) is passed to every model through trainControl(index = ...), so all models are compared on identical folds.
    • The baseline uses caret’s built-in "null" model (predicts the training mean), so it goes through the same folds as the learners.
    • A custom summaryFunction scores CV with the same RMSE, MAE and R² = 1 − SS_res/SS_tot definitions as the test evaluation. caret’s default R² is the squared correlation, which is undefined for the constant baseline.
    • Grids exactly as in D-008/D-010. XGBoost (optional M5) was not added.
    • Learning curves: 7 sizes × 20 repeats × 5 models = 700 refits with frozen hyperparameters (D-016).
    • Checked every figure visually. The F11 labels were unreadable on dark cells, so they now switch to white.
    • Re-running gives identical T03, T04 and learning-curve tables. Runtime is about 40 s.
  • Observations for the report (no modelling choice was changed):
    • SVR’s best σ = 0.01 is the smallest value in the grid (a smooth, nearly linear kernel), and RF’s best mtry = 5 uses all features. Both sit at the edge of their grids.
    • In the learning curves (F12), test-set RMSE at n = 80 is clearly higher than CV RMSE for the linear and SVR models. Phase 7’s residual plots should show whether one or two test galaxies cause this.
  • Owner decision: Accepted. The owner committed it.
  • Resulting code: R/05_train.R; randomForest and kernlab added to renv.lock
  • Effect on data: none (models saved to outputs/models/, git-ignored)
  • Linked decision: D-008, D-010, D-014, D-016
9.0.0.2.9 AI-009 — Test-set evaluation
  • Date: 2026-10-18
  • Stage: Evaluation (code)
  • Tool / model: Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5)
  • Input given to AI: the saved models and test.csv (via the script).
  • Prompt (short): “Write and run R/06_evaluate.R (test metrics with bootstrap CIs, T05, test_predictions.csv, F14–F17).”
  • AI output / suggestion:
    • Wrote R/06_evaluate.R. It predicts with the saved models unchanged, computes RMSE, MAE, R², bias, σ_NMAD and η (utils_metrics.R) and 95% percentile bootstrap CIs (2000 resamples, seed 42) for RMSE, R² and σ_NMAD. It writes T05 and test_predictions.csv and draws F14–F17. A re-run gives byte-identical tables.
    • Checked every figure visually and fixed label overlaps in F14 and F17.
    • Diagnosed why test RMSE is higher than CV RMSE for the linear model and SVR, using the largest-|Δz| list the script prints and a one-off check of feature ranges (not part of the pipeline). One test galaxy (1237661950779588703) has a red u − g but g − r, r − i and i − z at the blue edge of the training set, with r − i below the training minimum. The linear model and the near-linear SVR extrapolate and predict a negative redshift for it. Random-forest predictions are averages of training redshifts, so they cannot leave the training range, which is why RF has the lowest test RMSE. In total, 4 of the 20 test galaxies have at least one colour outside the training range.
    • All learners predict the lowest-z test galaxy too high: no training galaxy is that close, so predictions are pulled towards the mean (F15).
  • Owner decision: Accepted. The owner committed it. No modelling choice was changed after seeing the test results (AGENTS.md R5).
  • Notes for the report: the 95% CIs overlap heavily, so with only 20 test galaxies no model is clearly better than another. The CV ranking (SVR ≈ LM > RF > k-NN) differs from the test ranking (RF best). Report both and explain the extrapolation effect. Negative z_phot is unphysical, and that belongs in Limitations.
  • Resulting code: R/06_evaluate.R
  • Effect on data: none (read-only)
  • Linked decision: D-011, D-014
9.0.0.2.10 AI-010 — Physics interpretation
  • Date: 2026-10-18
  • Stage: Interpretation (code)

  • AI output / suggestion:
    • T06 combines RF permutation importance (%IncMSE) with standardised LM coefficients, their 95% CIs and p-values, and ranks each. F18 shows both side by side, built with patchwork. F19 shows the RF partial dependence on g − r and r − i (pdp, training data only).
    • interpretation_notes.md turns H1–H4 into verdicts computed from the tables, so the report does not depend on typed-in numbers. H3 has three outcomes (supported, partly supported, not supported) and names the models, rather than a single yes or no.
    • Added an interpretation line about u − g. It barely correlates with z on its own but is the second most important feature, with a negative coefficient at fixed g − r. The AI’s explanation: u − g traces galaxy type, which separates intrinsic redness from redshift reddening in g − r. This is a physical interpretation for the owner to check, not a tested result.
    • Checked F18 and F19 visually. The script runs without warnings, and a re-run gives byte-identical T06 and notes.
  • Owner decision: Accepted. The owner committed it.

9.0.0.2.14 AI-014 — Static web demo for free hosting
  • Date: 2026-10-22
  • Stage: Web demo (code)
  • Tool / model: Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5)
  • Input given to AI: the trained models, the train/test CSVs and T05.
  • Prompt (short): “Deploy for zero rupees at a single URL, drag and drop (e.g. Netlify), with a clean, demo-ready UI, as simple as possible but accurate.”
  • AI output / suggestion:
    • Checked the official hosting docs (Oct 2026):
      • Netlify Drop is free (300 credits a month) and deploys by dragging a folder, but serves static files only, so it cannot run R.
      • Posit Connect Cloud is free only for public repos (the owner’s repo is private).
      • shinyapps.io allows 25 active hours a month.
      • Hugging Face no longer offers free R Shiny.
    • Proposed and built a static demo (D-017). R/08_export_web.R exports the models’ parameters to site/model.js, and site/predict.js replays only the prediction step.
    • Verification: tests/testthat/test-web.R runs predict.js in R’s V8 engine. The first run caught a real export bug: SVR support vectors were truncated by [[1]], which made the SVR return a constant. It also caught a test-harness rounding issue and a wrong remembered reference value for lookback time. After the fixes, all four models reproduce R’s predictions for every test galaxy to within 1e-9, the out-of-range flags match R, and the distances match integrate().
    • The UI follows the frontend-design skill (“observatory at night” theme):
      • inputs for the five magnitudes, colour-coded by filter wavelength;
      • z with a light-travel time and distance from flat ΛCDM (H0 = 70, Ωm = 0.3), and v ≈ cz;
      • an animated schematic spectrum whose 4000 Å break slides through the filters;
      • all four models side by side, with RF recommended;
      • a training-range warning, and negative z flagged as unphysical;
      • a g − r against z context plot, and a “random SDSS galaxy” button (held-out test galaxies, showing their true z).
    • Tested in a browser at desktop and phone widths: the problem galaxy (Linear and SVR negative, RF 0.0903), invalid input, the random button, and no console errors. Fixed a hidden-label overlap in the spectrum and small chart text on phones.
    • Added 08_export_web.R to run_all.R; README Quick start and §11.2; V8 added to renv.lock, and the unused rsconnect removed.

9.0.0.2.15 AI-015 — Dataset version v2: 20 more training galaxies
  • Date: 2026-11-26

  • AI output / suggestion:

    • Inspection of batch 2: no NA, sentinels or duplicates, and no overlap with batch 1. The frozen 5·MAD rule removed 2 galaxies with very blue i − z (−5.7 and −16.6 MAD; the second, at z = 0.015, also has r − i at −6.0 MAD), like the 2 removed from batch 1 (AI-004). KS tests against batch 1 found no difference in redshift, r, g − r or u − g (smallest p = 0.16).
    • Made every script version-aware (PHOTOZ_VERSION, version_paths()), moved the v1 outputs to outputs/v1/ and data/processed/v1/, and re-ran v1 to prove it is byte-identical (every table and processed CSV has the same MD5, except one path string in T02).
    • Wrote R/09_compare_versions.R: a paired bootstrap of ΔRMSE on the shared test set (T07), hyperparameter drift (T08), F21 and F22, and computed notes. The AI found and fixed its own bug: a tibble() column named d_rmse shadowed the bootstrap vector, which made the CIs collapse to a point.
    • Result: k-NN improved clearly (−12%, paired CI below zero; k re-tuned 8 → 11). RF −4% and linear +2% are within the noise; SVR +13% is within the noise. RF stays the best test model. The bias–variance interpretation in comparison_notes.md is the AI’s reading, for the owner to check.
    • Web demo: a first-visit dialog asks “Which model do you want to look at?” (v1 · 100 / v2 · 120), with a persistent switch, ?model=v1|v2 links and per-version model files loaded on demand. The Shiny app got a model-set selector. Tests now cover both versions (174 passing); browser predictions equal R’s to 1e-9 for both.
  • Owner decision: pending review. v2 exceeds the brief’s 100-observation limit, so the owner should confirm with the instructor which version to submit (v1 is the compliant one).

  • Effect on data: new frozen raw file data/raw/sdss_raw_batch2.csv; v1 data unchanged; new data/processed/v2/
